title: What Being a Grandparent in 1960 Was Really Like

scenes.text: If you grew up in the fifties or sixties, close your eyes and picture your grandmother's house. The smell of something baking. A candy dish on the table. A clock ticking in the hallway. Crocheted doilies on every chair. And your grandmother, in a cotton housedress and an apron, waiting at the door to hug you. For millions of baby boomers, that house was the safest place in the world.
scenes.caption: GRANDMA'S HOUSE

scenes.text: But what was life like for the grandparents themselves? If you were a grandparent in nineteen sixty, you were probably born in the eighteen nineties or the first years of the nineteen hundreds. You had grown up with horses and buggies, oil lamps and outhouses. And now you were watching your grandchildren grow up with television, jet airplanes and rockets to space.
scenes.caption: BORN IN THE 1890s

scenes.text: Today, let's look at the world through their eyes. The grandparents of the baby boom. What they had lived through, how they lived in nineteen sixty, and what they gave their grandchildren. If you had grandparents like these, I think you'll see them clearly by the end.
scenes.caption: THROUGH THEIR EYES

scenes.text: Think about what a grandparent of nineteen sixty had already lived through. As children, many had no electricity, no telephone and no car. They were teenagers or young adults during the First World War. Many young men served in France in nineteen seventeen and eighteen. And then came the influenza pandemic of nineteen eighteen, which killed about six hundred and seventy-five thousand Americans.
scenes.caption: THEY HAD LIVED THROUGH IT ALL

scenes.text: Then came the Great Depression. Many of them were in their thirties when the stock market crashed in nineteen twenty-nine. They lost jobs, farms, savings and homes. They raised their children on beans, bread and hand-me-downs. Many never fully trusted banks again, and kept cash hidden in coffee cans, mattresses and cookie jars for the rest of their lives.
scenes.caption: THE GREAT DEPRESSION

scenes.text: And then the Second World War, when they sent their own sons off to fight, and hung a blue star in the window. Some of those stars turned gold. By nineteen sixty, they had survived two world wars, a pandemic and a depression. No wonder they seemed so calm about the small problems of their grandchildren.
scenes.caption: A STAR IN THE WINDOW

scenes.text: They had also seen the world change faster than any generation before. They had seen the first automobiles, the first airplanes, the first radios and the first movies with sound. They had watched electric lights come to their towns, and indoor plumbing come to their homes. Some of them had seen their first television set only a few years earlier, in their sixties.
scenes.caption: THEY SAW IT ALL CHANGE

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty, many grandparents still lived in the old family home. A big farmhouse, or a two-story house in an older part of town, with a front porch, a big kitchen and a garden out back. They had lived there for thirty or forty years. Every room was full of memories, and nothing ever changed.
scenes.query: 1950s old two story house front porch
scenes.caption: THE OLD FAMILY HOME

scenes.text: Many others lived with their grown children. It was common for a widowed grandmother to move in with her son or daughter's family. She might have a small bedroom upstairs, or a room off the kitchen. She helped cook, watched the children and told stories. Three generations under one roof was a normal part of American life.
scenes.caption: THREE GENERATIONS

scenes.text: Some grandparents moved to Florida or Arizona, but in nineteen sixty, that was still unusual. Most stayed close to home, close to their church and their friends, and close to their grandchildren. On Sundays, the whole family came over for dinner. The grandparents' house was the center of the family.
scenes.caption: THE CENTER OF THE FAMILY

scenes.text: Money was tight for many grandparents in nineteen sixty. Social Security had only started paying monthly benefits in nineteen forty, and in nineteen sixty, the average check for a retired worker was about seventy-four dollars a month. Many older people had no pension at all. And there was no Medicare yet. That wouldn't come until nineteen sixty-five.
scenes.caption: $74 A MONTH

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-nine, about one in three Americans over sixty-five lived in poverty. Many depended on their children for help. Others kept working as long as their bodies allowed, as farmers, shopkeepers, carpenters or seamstresses. The idea of retiring at sixty-five and traveling the world was still new.
scenes.caption: ONE IN THREE WAS POOR

scenes.text: But they were masters at making do. Grandmothers saved string, rubber bands, bread bags, aluminum foil and buttons. They mended socks, patched clothes, and made quilts from scraps. They grew vegetables and canned them. Nothing was thrown away that might be useful someday. Use it up, wear it out, make it do, or do without.
scenes.caption: USE IT UP, WEAR IT OUT

scenes.text: Many grandparents also had firm opinions about money. Never buy what you can't pay cash for. Always keep something put away for a rainy day. Don't trust anything that sounds too good to be true. They watched their grown children buy cars and televisions on credit, and shook their heads. Their grandchildren didn't always listen, but many later wished they had.
scenes.caption: PAY CASH

scenes.text: What was a day like for a grandmother in nineteen sixty? She rose early, out of a lifetime's habit. She cooked a big breakfast, with eggs, bacon, biscuits and coffee boiled in an old pot. She swept the porch, fed the chickens if she had them, and worked in her garden while it was still cool.
scenes.caption: UP EARLY

scenes.text: In the afternoon, she might bake. Bread, pies, cookies, cakes. Many grandmothers never measured anything. A handful of this, a pinch of that, until it looked right. Their grandchildren later tried to write down the recipes, and found it almost impossible. The secret ingredient, many said, was the grandmother herself.
scenes.caption: SHE NEVER MEASURED

scenes.text: In the evening, she listened to the radio or watched television. Lawrence Welk on Saturday nights was a favorite of many grandparents. So were Ed Sullivan, Gunsmoke and religious programs. She read the Bible, did crossword puzzles, and wrote letters to her children and grandchildren in careful, flowing cursive.
scenes.caption: LAWRENCE WELK

scenes.text: And she went to church. For many grandmothers, the church was the center of life outside the home. Sunday services, Wednesday prayer meetings, the ladies' aid society, the quilting circle and the church suppers. She brought casseroles to every funeral and pies to every bake sale. Her faith had carried her through the hardest times, and she never let go of it.
scenes.caption: HER FAITH

scenes.text: Grandfathers of nineteen sixty were often quiet men with strong hands. Many had worked on farms, in mines, on railroads or in factories since they were boys. They had pocket watches and suspenders, and a pocketknife they used for everything. Many chewed tobacco or smoked a pipe.
scenes.caption: STRONG HANDS

scenes.text: Grandpa might spend his mornings in the workshop, fixing things for the neighbors. His afternoons might be at the barbershop, the feed store or the courthouse square, where the old men gathered on benches to talk about the weather, the crops and the old days. In the evening, he sat on the porch in his rocking chair.
scenes.query: 1950s old men sitting bench town square
scenes.caption: THE BENCH ON THE SQUARE

scenes.text: He took the grandchildren fishing. He taught them to whittle, to bait a hook, to drive a nail and to whistle. He told stories about the war, or the Depression, or what the town looked like before the paved roads came. And he slipped them a quarter or a stick of gum when their parents weren't looking.
scenes.caption: GONE FISHING

scenes.text: Grandparents also had very definite ideas about manners. Children said yes ma'am and no sir. You didn't speak at the table unless spoken to. You wrote a thank-you note for every gift, in your best handwriting. You stood up when an adult entered the room. And if you forgot, you heard about it, gently but firmly.
scenes.caption: YES MA'AM

scenes.text: For the grandchildren, visits to grandma's house were magical. The cookie jar was always full. The rules were looser. Grandma let you stay up late, eat dessert first, and lick the bowl. You slept in a big feather bed under a handmade quilt. In the morning, you woke up to the smell of bacon and fresh coffee.
scenes.caption: THE COOKIE JAR

scenes.text: The house was full of interesting things. An old trunk in the attic with army uniforms and love letters. A pump organ in the parlor. A wind-up Victrola with old records. Photographs of stern-looking ancestors on the walls. A button tin, full of every button ever saved, that children could sort for hours.
scenes.caption: THE BUTTON TIN

scenes.text: Many grandparents also spoke another language. German, Italian, Polish, Swedish, Yiddish, Czech or Spanish. They had come to America as children, or their parents had. They spoke English with an accent, and switched to the old language when they didn't want the children to understand. Their grandchildren often learned a few words, mostly the ones they weren't supposed to.
scenes.caption: THE OLD LANGUAGE

scenes.text: And grandparents connected children to history. A boy in nineteen sixty might have a grandfather who had seen Civil War veterans march in parades. A girl might have a grandmother who remembered when women couldn't vote. Women won the right to vote in nineteen twenty, and many grandmothers of nineteen sixty had cast their very first ballot that year.
scenes.caption: SHE REMEMBERED

scenes.text: Holidays belonged to the grandparents. Thanksgiving and Christmas dinners at grandma's house were huge, with every aunt, uncle and cousin crammed into the dining room, and the kids at a card table in the kitchen. Grandma cooked for days beforehand. The turkey, the stuffing, the pies, and her famous rolls.
scenes.caption: THE KIDS' TABLE

scenes.text: After dinner, the men fell asleep in front of the football game. The women washed dishes and talked in the kitchen. The cousins ran wild outside, or explored the attic. And grandpa told the same stories he told every year, and everyone listened anyway.
scenes.caption: THE SAME STORIES

scenes.text: At Christmas, grandparents often gave practical gifts. Hand-knitted mittens and scarves. Socks. A savings bond, which the grandchildren didn't appreciate until years later. A crisp dollar bill in a card. And maybe one special toy, bought after weeks of saving. Those simple gifts are often the ones grandchildren remember the most.
scenes.caption: A SAVINGS BOND

scenes.text: Growing old in nineteen sixty was harder than today in many ways. Life expectancy at birth was about seventy years. Heart disease, strokes and cancer took many people in their sixties. Hearing aids were big and clumsy. Eyeglasses were thick. And there were fewer treatments for the problems of old age.
scenes.caption: HARDER IN MANY WAYS

scenes.text: When grandparents grew too old or sick to live alone, they usually moved in with their children. Nursing homes existed, but they were much less common than today. Families took care of their own. Daughters, especially, cared for aging parents, often for years. It was simply expected.
scenes.caption: FAMILIES TOOK CARE OF THEIR OWN

scenes.text: And when a grandparent died, the funeral was often held in the family home, or at the local funeral parlor, with a wake the night before. The whole town came. Neighbors brought food. Children saw death up close, as a natural part of life. And the old house was sold, and the family scattered a little more.
scenes.caption: THE WHOLE TOWN CAME

scenes.text: So what did the grandparents of nineteen sixty give us? They gave us roots. A connection to a world that was already disappearing. They gave us their stories, their recipes, their quilts and their values. Hard work. Thrift. Faith. Family. Not complaining.
scenes.caption: THEY GAVE US ROOTS

scenes.text: And many of us didn't realize how much they meant until they were gone. We wish we had asked more questions. Written down the recipes. Recorded their voices. Learned the old language. If your grandparents are still in your memory, maybe it's time to write down what you remember, for your own grandchildren.
scenes.caption: WRITE IT DOWN

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What do you remember most about your grandparents? What did your grandmother cook, and what did your grandfather teach you? We read every comment, and we'd love to hear about them. Next time, we're looking at what a dollar really bought in nineteen fifty-eight. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: TELL US ABOUT THEM
